claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The starting material has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The starting material exhibits limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
Introducing 5–10 vol% of a ductile phase is the proposed intervention.
The proposed ductile-phase particles have a size of 100–500 nm.
The ductile-phase particles are to be distributed along grain boundaries.
The intervention will overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness.
The intervention will retain or increase tensile strength.
The ductile-phase reinforcements will act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The grain-boundary reinforcements will reduce dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will reduce local stress concentrations.
The intervention will mitigate microcracking and catastrophic damage during straining.
The predicted performance applies under room-temperature tensile testing.
The predicted performance applies at a tensile strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
Elongation at break is predicted to rise from 5% in the untreated material to 6.5–7.5% after treatment.
The predicted elongation change is described as a 20–30% increase.
Strength is predicted to rise from 1000 MPa in the untreated material to 1100–1200 MPa after treatment.
The predicted strength change is a 10–20% increase.
The intervention may not apply to alloy systems or microstructures other than eutectic high-entropy alloys with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The hypothesis is designated as falsified if ductility increases by less than 10% or strength increases by less than 5% relative to the untreated control.

contradictions.description: An increase from 5% elongation to 6.5–7.5% corresponds to a 30–50% relative increase, not the stated 20–30% increase.

The prediction requires a 20–30% ductility increase and a 10–20% strength increase, but the falsification thresholds are below 10% and below 5%, respectively. Intermediate results can miss the predicted outcome without falsifying the hypothesis.
